Why Do I Keep Getting Infections Around Old Dental Work?

Written By

Dental Implants Team

Introduction

If you've experienced recurring discomfort, swelling, or signs of infection around old dental work, you're certainly not alone. It's one of the most common concerns that brings patients back to the dental chair â€” and one of the most frequently searched dental topics online. Many people wonder why a filling, crown, or bridge that seemed perfectly fine for years has suddenly become a source of trouble.

Infections around old dental work can develop for a number of reasons, and understanding the possible causes is an important first step toward finding the right solution. Dental restorations, while designed to be durable, do not last indefinitely. Over time, materials can wear, seals can break down, and the underlying tooth structure may change â€” all of which can create conditions where bacteria may accumulate.

This article explores the common reasons why infections may recur around previous dental restorations, the signs and symptoms to be aware of, and when it may be appropriate to seek a professional dental assessment. Whether you have old fillings, crowns, or more complex restorations, the information here aims to help you make informed decisions about your oral health.

Why Do Infections Keep Occurring Around Old Dental Work?

Recurring infections around old dental work often occur because dental restorations can deteriorate over time, allowing bacteria to penetrate gaps between the restoration and the natural tooth. Ageing fillings, crowns, or bridges may develop micro-cracks or lose their seal, creating spaces where decay and infection can develop beneath the surface. A professional clinical assessment is needed to identify the specific cause and determine appropriate treatment.

Common Causes of Infections Around Old Dental Restorations

There are several reasons why old dental work may become associated with recurring infections. Understanding these causes can help you appreciate why early professional evaluation is so valuable.

Deterioration of dental materials. All dental restorations have a functional lifespan. Composite fillings, amalgam fillings, and dental crowns gradually wear down through years of biting, chewing, and exposure to temperature changes. As materials age, they may crack, chip, or shrink slightly, breaking the seal that once protected the underlying tooth.

Secondary decay (recurrent caries). When the margin between a restoration and the natural tooth begins to break down, bacteria can infiltrate the gap. This can lead to new decay forming beneath or around the existing restoration â€” often referred to as secondary or recurrent decay. Because this decay is hidden beneath the restoration, it may progress significantly before any symptoms appear.

Incomplete previous treatment. In some cases, the original dental work may not have fully addressed the extent of decay or infection. If bacteria remained in the tooth structure at the time of the initial restoration, infection may eventually recur.

Changes in bite or tooth structure. Over time, teeth can shift, crack, or experience structural changes that place additional stress on old restorations, potentially compromising their integrity.

Signs and Symptoms of Infection Around Old Dental Work

Recognising the early signs of a potential infection can help you seek timely advice. While symptoms can vary depending on the type of restoration and the extent of any underlying issue, there are several common indicators worth being aware of.

Persistent or recurring pain. A dull ache or sharp pain around a previously restored tooth â€” particularly one that seems to come and go â€” may suggest that something has changed beneath or around the restoration. Pain when biting down or sensitivity to hot and cold can also be relevant.

Swelling or tenderness. Swelling in the gum tissue surrounding an old filling, crown, or bridge may indicate that an infection is developing. The area may feel tender to the touch or appear reddened.

An unpleasant taste or odour. A persistent bad taste in the mouth, particularly around a specific tooth, can sometimes be associated with infection or decay beneath dental work.

A visible gap or loose restoration. If you can see a gap between your tooth and a filling or crown, or if a restoration feels loose or moves slightly, this may indicate that the seal has been compromised.

A small bump on the gum (dental abscess). A pimple-like swelling on the gum near an old restoration may indicate a dental abscess, which requires prompt professional attention â€” contact us to arrange an urgent assessment.

It's important to note that some infections develop without any obvious symptoms in the early stages, which is one reason why regular dental check-ups remain so important.

The Science Behind Recurring Dental Infections

To understand why infections recur around old dental work, it helps to know a little about tooth anatomy and how bacteria interact with dental restorations.

A natural tooth consists of several layers. The outer layer â€” enamel â€” is the hardest substance in the human body and serves as the primary barrier against bacteria. Beneath the enamel lies dentine, a softer and more porous layer that contains microscopic tubules leading toward the pulp â€” the innermost part of the tooth that houses nerves and blood vessels.

When a tooth is restored with a filling or crown, the restoration replaces lost enamel or dentine and creates an artificial seal. However, unlike natural enamel, this seal is a junction between two different materials â€” the restoration and the tooth. This junction, known as the margin, is inherently more vulnerable to bacterial infiltration than intact enamel.

Over years of use, thermal expansion and contraction (from hot and cold foods), mechanical stress from chewing, and gradual chemical breakdown can all cause marginal deterioration. Once bacteria breach the margin, they enter the dentine layer, where they can spread relatively quickly through the tubules toward the pulp.

If bacteria reach the pulp, they can cause pulpitis (inflammation of the pulp) and eventually a periapical infection â€” an infection at the root tip that may lead to abscess formation. This process can occur silently over months or even years, which is why infections around old dental work sometimes appear to develop suddenly despite having been building gradually.

Why Some Patients Experience Repeated Infections

Some patients seem more prone to recurring infections around old dental work than others. While every case is unique and requires individual clinical assessment, there are several factors that may contribute to a pattern of repeated issues.

Multiple old restorations. Patients who had significant dental work carried out many years ago may find that several restorations begin to fail within a similar timeframe, as the materials reach the end of their functional life.

Oral hygiene challenges. Areas around old dental work can sometimes be more difficult to clean effectively. Rough or overhanging margins on fillings, or gaps beneath bridge pontics, can harbour plaque and bacteria despite diligent brushing and flossing.

Grinding or clenching (bruxism). Habitual teeth grinding or clenching places considerable additional force on dental restorations, accelerating wear and increasing the likelihood of cracks or fractures in both the restoration and the underlying tooth.

Underlying gum disease. Periodontal disease can affect the supporting structures around restored teeth, leading to gum recession, bone loss, and increased exposure of vulnerable root surfaces near old restorations. Maintaining healthy gums through appropriate periodontal care is an important part of protecting existing dental work.

Dry mouth. Reduced saliva flow â€” whether caused by medication, medical conditions, or other factors â€” diminishes the mouth's natural defence against bacteria and can increase the risk of decay around restorations.

Treatment Approaches for Infections Around Old Dental Work

The appropriate treatment for an infection around old dental work depends entirely on the specific cause, the extent of any damage, and the overall condition of the tooth. A thorough clinical examination, often including dental X-rays, is necessary to determine the most suitable approach.

Replacement of the restoration. If the existing filling or crown has deteriorated but the underlying tooth remains structurally sound, removing the old restoration, clearing any decay, and placing a new restoration may resolve the issue.

Root canal treatment. If infection has spread to the pulp of the tooth, root canal treatment may be recommended. This involves removing the infected pulp tissue, cleaning and shaping the root canals, and sealing the tooth to prevent further infection.

Treatment of gum disease. If periodontal disease is contributing to the problem, targeted gum treatment may be necessary alongside any restorative work.

Extraction and replacement. In cases where the tooth is too severely compromised to be saved, extraction may be the most appropriate option. Following extraction, there are several options for replacing the missing tooth, including dental implants, which can provide a long-term, stable replacement.

It is worth emphasising that the right treatment path varies from patient to patient. What works well for one person may not be suitable for another, which is why an individual clinical assessment is always essential.

When Professional Dental Assessment May Be Needed

While not every twinge or moment of sensitivity around old dental work necessarily indicates an infection, there are certain situations where seeking a professional evaluation sooner rather than later is sensible.

You may wish to arrange a dental assessment if you experience:

  • Persistent pain around a previously restored tooth that does not resolve within a few days
  • Swelling in the gum, cheek, or jaw near old dental work
  • Sensitivity to hot or cold that lingers after the stimulus is removed
  • A loose or visibly damaged restoration such as a cracked filling or a crown that moves
  • A recurring bad taste or unpleasant odour from around a specific tooth
  • A small bump or swelling on the gum near an old restoration
  • Difficulty chewing or a feeling that your bite has changed around a restored tooth

These symptoms do not automatically confirm an infection, but they can indicate that something may have changed and warrants professional investigation. Early assessment often means that less invasive treatment options may be available.

There is no need to feel anxious about seeking advice. A dental professional can carry out a thorough examination and explain any findings clearly, helping you understand your options without pressure.

Prevention and Oral Health Advice

While it is not always possible to prevent every issue with old dental work, there are practical steps you can take to help protect your restorations and reduce the risk of infection.

Maintain a thorough oral hygiene routine. Brushing twice daily with a fluoride toothpaste and cleaning between your teeth with interdental brushes or floss helps remove plaque from around restorations. Pay particular attention to the gum line and the margins of fillings and crowns.

Attend regular dental check-ups. Routine examinations allow your dentist to monitor the condition of existing restorations and identify early signs of deterioration before problems develop. X-rays taken at appropriate intervals can reveal hidden decay or changes beneath the surface.

Address grinding or clenching habits. If you grind your teeth, discuss this with your dentist. A custom-made night guard may help protect both your natural teeth and your restorations from excessive wear.

Be mindful of your diet. Limiting sugary and acidic foods and drinks reduces the bacterial activity that contributes to decay around restorations. Drinking water regularly also helps maintain a healthy oral environment.

Don't ignore early symptoms. If you notice any changes around old dental work â€” even minor ones â€” mentioning them at your next dental appointment allows your dentist to investigate early, when issues are typically easier to manage.

Key Points to Remember

  • Old dental restorations can deteriorate over time, potentially allowing bacteria to reach the underlying tooth structure.
  • Secondary decay beneath old fillings and crowns is a common cause of recurring infections and may develop without obvious symptoms initially.
  • Symptoms such as persistent pain, swelling, sensitivity, or a bad taste around old dental work warrant professional assessment.
  • Treatment options vary depending on the cause and extent of the problem, ranging from restoration replacement to root canal treatment or extraction.
  • Good oral hygiene, regular dental check-ups, and early attention to symptoms are the most effective ways to protect existing dental work.
  • Every patient's situation is unique â€” a clinical examination is always necessary to determine the most appropriate course of action.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long do dental fillings and crowns typically last?

The lifespan of a dental restoration depends on several factors, including the material used, the size and location of the restoration, your oral hygiene habits, and the forces placed on the tooth. Composite fillings may last between five and fifteen years, while well-maintained crowns can often last ten to twenty years or longer. However, these are general estimates. Some restorations may need replacing sooner, while others may remain functional for much longer. Regular dental check-ups help monitor the condition of your restorations and identify any that may be approaching the end of their functional life.

Can an infection under old dental work spread to other teeth?

An untreated dental infection has the potential to affect surrounding tissues and, in some circumstances, adjacent teeth. Bacteria from an infected tooth can spread through the bone and gum tissue. In rare cases, a dental infection may cause more widespread health concerns. This is one reason why seeking professional advice when symptoms arise is important. With appropriate treatment, most dental infections can be effectively managed before they have an opportunity to affect other areas.

Is it normal to have pain around an old filling?

Occasional mild sensitivity around an old filling is not uncommon, particularly in response to temperature changes. However, persistent or worsening pain, sharp pain when biting, or prolonged sensitivity to hot or cold may suggest that the restoration has deteriorated or that decay or infection may be developing beneath it. If you experience ongoing discomfort around an old filling, it is sensible to have it assessed by a dental professional to determine whether any treatment is needed.

Can I prevent infections around old dental work?

While not all issues with old dental work can be prevented, maintaining excellent oral hygiene, attending regular dental check-ups, and addressing any early symptoms promptly can significantly reduce the risk of infection. Avoiding excessive consumption of sugary foods and drinks, and using fluoride toothpaste, helps protect the margins of restorations where bacteria are most likely to infiltrate. If you grind your teeth, a protective night guard may help reduce the stress placed on your restorations.

Should old dental work be replaced before problems develop?

This is a decision best made in consultation with your dentist following a clinical examination. Proactively replacing a restoration that shows signs of wear, marginal breakdown, or early deterioration may prevent more complex problems from developing later. However, if a restoration remains well-sealed and functionally sound, there may be no clinical reason to replace it. Your dentist can advise you based on the specific condition of each restoration and your individual circumstances.

What happens if I ignore signs of infection around old dental work?

Delaying professional assessment when signs of infection are present may allow the problem to progress. What might initially require a relatively straightforward restoration replacement could develop into an issue requiring root canal treatment, or in some cases, tooth extraction. Early intervention generally offers more conservative treatment options and better outcomes. If you notice any concerning symptoms, arranging a dental appointment is a sensible step.

Conclusion

Recurring infections around old dental work are a common concern, and understanding why they occur can help you take informed action. Dental restorations, while durable, are subject to wear and deterioration over time. When the seal between a restoration and the natural tooth breaks down, bacteria can gain access to vulnerable tooth structures, potentially leading to decay and infection.

The good news is that with regular dental monitoring, good oral hygiene practices, and prompt attention to any emerging symptoms, many of these issues can be identified and addressed before they become more complex. Whether the solution involves replacing an ageing filling, carrying out root canal treatment, or considering alternative options, there are effective pathways to restoring your oral health.

If you are experiencing persistent symptoms around old dental work â€” such as pain, swelling, sensitivity, or a recurring bad taste â€” seeking a professional dental assessment is a worthwhile step. Your dentist can examine the area thoroughly, explain their findings, and discuss the options available to you.

Dental symptoms and treatment options should always be assessed individually during a clinical examination.

Looking after your existing dental work is an investment in your long-term oral health, and staying informed is one of the best things you can do for your smile.

This article is intended for general educational purposes and does not constitute clinical advice. Treatment suitability depends on individual assessment by a qualified dental professional.
